protocol.source_text:
CLINICAL FEATURES 
Symptoms 
*RUQ pain / epigastric pain 
*Nausea 
*Vomiting 
*Anorexia 
*Low grade fever 
Signs 
*Vital signs parallel the degree of illness 
*± Jaundice 
*Epigastric / RUQ tenderness 
*Abdominal guarding 
*Murphy’s sign 
➔ inspiratory pause on palpation of RUQ 
*Search for complications & other sources of 
pain 
 
 
 
 
RISK FACTORS 
*Increasing age 
*Female 
*Parity 
*Family history 
*Obesity 
*Diabetes Mellitus 
*Profound weight loss 
*Fasting 
*Cystic fibrosis 
*Malabsorption syndromes 
*Medications e.g. antibiotics, lipid lowering, 
diuretics, oestrogen-containing, steroids 
 
ED MANAGEMENT 
The primary goal of ED care is resuscitation, stabilization and an 
expedient diagnosis 
RESUSCITATION 
*ABC approach 
*IV line – 20mls/kg Balsol/Ringer’s Lactate fluid bolus if shocked 
INVESTIGATIONS 
*Bedside 
ECG, blood gas, U-dipstix, U-ßHCG, POCUS (see ultrasound features box) 
*Laboratory 
FBC, U&E, CRP, CMP, LFT, amylase, lipase, ±INR/PTT, ±blood 
cultures 
*Radiological 
X-rays – CXR erect, AXR supine & erect 
Abdominal ultrasound 
CT Abdomen – not test of choice and recommended only for the 
evaluation of abdominal pain if the diagnosis is uncertain 
SPECIFIC TREATMENT 
*Antibiotics – Augmentin® 1.2g stat IV 
*Antiemetics 
*Analgesia – see Pain Management in ED Protocol 
 
DISPOSITION 
*Urgent surgical referral 
COMPLICATIONS 
*Sepsis 
*Pancreatitis 
*Ascending cholangitis 
*Gallbladder empyema 
*Emphysematous cholecystitis 
*Gallbladder perforation – localized/free 
*Hepatitis 
*Choledocholithiasis 
 
 
 
 
ULTRASOUND FEATURES 
Gallstones/sludge and 1 or more of 
the following: 
*GB wall thickening (>4mm) 
(false positive in wall thickening found in 
ascites, CCF, carcinoma, hypoalbuminaemia) 
*GB distention 
(diameter >4cm, length >10cm) 
*Pericholecystic fluid 
*Dilated ducts ➔ CBD or intrahepatic 
*Air in the GB wall 
*Ultrasonographic Murphy sign 
➔  pain when the probe is pushed 
directly on the GB (not related to 
breathing)
